## Q1
Arrange these numbers in ascending order by the number of distinct prime factors.

A. 729<br>
B. 1001<br>
C. 1111<br>
D. 420

## Q1 - Options
(A) A, C, B, D
(B) D, A, B, C
(C) A, B, C, D
(D) D, A, C, B

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q47

Factor each number and count unique primes, not repeated powers: 729 = 3⁶ has 1; 1111 = 11 × 101 has 2; 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 has 3; and 420 = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 has 4. Sorting those counts from 1 to 4 gives A, C, B, D.

## Q2
In a group of 120 people, 65 eat rice, 45 eat bread, 42 eat curd, 20 eat both rice and bread, 25 eat both rice and curd, 15 eat both bread and curd, and 8 eat all three. How many eat at least one of the three items?

## Q2 - Options
(A) 56
(B) 100
(C) 92
(D) 65

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q1

Apply inclusion-exclusion: 65 + 45 + 42 - 20 - 25 - 15 + 8 = 100. The pairwise overlaps were subtracted once too often, so the triple overlap is added back once.

## Q3
For positive integers m and n, which statements are correct: n ≠ 1 implies m &lt; mn; a composite k can be written k = mn with 1 &lt; m,n &gt; k; mn = 1 implies m = n = 1; and a composite k can be written k = mn with 1 &lt; m,n &lt; k?

## Q3 - Options
(A) A, C, D only
(B) B, C, D only
(C) A, B only
(D) A, B, C

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q57

If n ≠ 1, positivity makes n at least 2, hence m &lt; mn. A product of positive integers can equal 1 only when both are 1. A composite number has proper factors strictly between 1 and k, so D is true; B is impossible because two factors greater than k cannot multiply to k.

## Q5
Seven people enter a lift. The lift stops only at three floors (which are unspecified). At each of the three floors, no one enters the lift, but at least one person leaves the lift. After the three floor stops, the lift is empty. In how many ways can this happen?

## Q5 - Options
(A) 1844
(B) 2187
(C) 1806
(D) 343

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q2

Each of the 7 people must leave the lift at exactly one of the 3 floor stops, and every stop needs at least one person, so this counts the number of onto (surjective) functions from a 7-element set to a 3-element set.

Total assignments without the "at least one" restriction: 3⁷ = 2187

Subtract assignments where at least one floor gets nobody, using inclusion-exclusion: 3⁷ − C(3,1)·2⁷ + C(3,2)·1⁷ = 2187 − 3(128) + 3(1) = 2187 − 384 + 3 = 1806

So there are 1806 valid ways, ruling out 2187 (which ignores the non-empty requirement) and 343 = 7³ (which wrongly treats floors as the objects being distributed).

## Q6
What is the minimum number of students in a discrete mathematics class to be sure that at least six will receive the same grade, if there are seven possible grades: S, A, B, C, D, P and F?

## Q6 - Options
(A) 7
(B) 13
(C) 36
(D) 14

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q4

The generalized pigeonhole principle states that to guarantee at least k items in one of n boxes, you need at least (k-1)·n + 1 items.

Here k = 6 (students sharing a grade) and n = 7 (grades), so the minimum count is (6-1)×7 + 1 = 35 + 1 = 36

With only 35 students, each grade could be given to exactly 5 students with no grade reaching 6, so 36 is the smallest number that forces at least one grade to repeat 6 times.

## Q7
Consider the following statements:

A. There exists a Boolean algebra with '5' elements.<br>
B. Every element of Boolean algebra has unique complement.<br>
C. If a Lattice 'L' is a Boolean algebra then 'L' is not relatively complemented.<br>
D. The direct product of two Boolean algebras is also a Boolean algebra.

Choose the correct answer about the four statements given above.

## Q7 - Options
(A) Only A and D are correct
(B) Only B and D are correct
(C) All statements are NOT correct
(D) All statements are correct

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q42

Check each statement against Boolean algebra theorems.

- **A** — Every finite Boolean algebra has exactly 2ⁿ elements for some n, so its size must be a power of 2. Since 5 is not a power of 2, no Boolean algebra with 5 elements exists, so A is false.
- **B** — Uniqueness of the complement is a fundamental theorem of Boolean algebra, so B is true.
- **C** — A Boolean algebra is in fact always a relatively complemented distributive lattice, so claiming it is not relatively complemented is false.
- **D** — The direct product of two Boolean algebras, with operations defined componentwise, is itself a Boolean algebra, so D is true.

Only B and D are correct.

## Q8
Which statements about the floor and ceiling functions are correct?

Statement I: floor(2x) = floor(x) + floor(x + 1/2) for every real number x.<br>
Statement II: ceil(x + y) = ceil(x) + ceil(y) for all real numbers x and y.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q8 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are false
(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false
(D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q22

Statement I is the standard Hermite identity floor(2x) = floor(x) + floor(x + 1/2), valid for all real x. Statement II is false: for x = y = 0.5, ceil(1) = 1 but ceil(0.5) + ceil(0.5) = 2.

## Q9
How many ways are there to assign 5 different jobs to 4 different employees if every employee is assigned at least one job?

## Q9 - Options
(A) 1024
(B) 625
(C) 240
(D) 20

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q23

This counts onto (surjective) functions from a 5-element set to a 4-element set: 4! x S(5,4) = 24 x 10 = 240. Equivalently: pick the employee who gets 2 jobs (4 ways), pick those 2 jobs (C(5,2) = 10), assign the remaining 3 jobs to 3 employees (3! = 6): 4 x 10 x 6 = 240.

## Q10
A warehouse stores products in bins identified by aisle, location within the aisle, and shelf. There are 50 aisles, 85 locations per aisle, and 5 shelves. What is the least number of products the company can have so that at least two products must be stored in the same bin?

## Q10 - Options
(A) 251
(B) 426
(C) 4251
(D) 21251

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q24

Total bins = 50 x 85 x 5 = 21,250. By the pigeonhole principle, one more product than the number of bins forces two products into the same bin: 21,250 + 1 = 21,251.

## Q11
A person climbing stairs can take either one stair or two stairs at a time. In how many ways can this person climb a flight of eight stairs?

## Q11 - Options
(A) 21
(B) 24
(C) 31
(D) 34

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q25

The last move is either a single stair (leaving f(n-1) ways to reach the previous stair) or a double stair (leaving f(n-2) ways), so f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2), the Fibonacci recurrence. Starting from f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2, the values continue 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and finally f(8) = 34.

## Q12
The number of positive integers not exceeding 100 that are either odd or the square of an integer is \_\_\_\_.

## Q12 - Options
(A) 63
(B) 59
(C) 55
(D) 50

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q1

There are 50 odd integers through 100. Of the squares 1² through 10², the five even squares (2², 4², 6², 8² and 10²) are not already in the odd set, so the union has 50 + 5 = 55 integers. Counting all ten squares again would double-count the five odd squares.

## Q13
How many ways are there to pack six copies of the same book into four identical boxes, where a box can contain as many as six books?

## Q13 - Options
(A) 4
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 9

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q2

Because both books and boxes are identical, each arrangement is a partition of 6 into at most four positive parts. The nine partitions are 6; 5+1; 4+2; 4+1+1; 3+3; 3+2+1; 3+1+1+1; 2+2+2; and 2+2+1+1.

## Q15
Let a²ᶜ mod n = (aᶜ)² mod n and a²ᶜ⁺¹ mod n = a·(aᶜ)² mod n. For a = 7, b = 17 and n = 561, what is the value of aᵇ(mod n)?

## Q15 - Options
(A) 160
(B) 166
(C) 157
(D) 67

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q37

Compute 7¹⁷ mod 561 using modular exponentiation with binary exponent 17 = 16 + 1:

1. Repeated squaring:<br>
   7¹ mod 561 = 7<br>
   7² mod 561 = 49<br>
   7⁴ mod 561 = 49² = 2401 = 4 × 561 + 157 = 157<br>
   7⁸ mod 561 = 157² = 24649 = 43 × 561 + 526 ≡ -35 mod 561<br>
   7¹⁶ mod 561 = (-35)² = 1225 = 2 × 561 + 103 = 103
2. Multiply terms:<br>
   7¹⁷ mod 561 = (7¹⁶ × 7¹) mod 561 = (103 × 7) mod 561 = 721 mod 561<br>
   721 - 561 = 160

## Q16
How many cards must be selected from a standard deck of 52 cards to guarantee that at least three hearts are present among them?

## Q16 - Options
(A) 10
(B) 13
(C) 17
(D) 42

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q48

Using worst-case analysis via the Pigeonhole Principle:

A standard deck of 52 cards contains:<br>
13 hearts<br>
39 non-heart cards (spades, clubs, diamonds).

To guarantee drawing at least 3 hearts, consider the worst-case distribution where all non-heart cards are drawn before any additional hearts are selected:<br>
39 non-hearts + 3 hearts = 42 cards total.

Selecting 42 cards ensures that at least 3 cards must be hearts.

## Q17
Consider the Euler’s phi function given by φ(n) = n ∏(1 - 1/p)<br>
where p runs over all the primes dividing n. What is the value of φ(45)?

## Q17 - Options
(A) 3
(B) 12
(C) 6
(D) 24

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q61

Computing Euler's totient function for n = 45:

Prime factorization of 45 is:<br>
45 = 3^2 \* 5.<br>
The distinct prime factors dividing 45 are p = 3 and p = 5.

Applying Euler's product formula:<br>
phi(45) = 45 \* (1 - 1/3) \* (1 - 1/5)<br>
phi(45) = 45 \* (2/3) \* (4/5)<br>
phi(45) = 45 \* (8/15) = 3 \* 8 = 24.

## Q18
How many bit strings of length ten either start with a 1 bit or end with two bits 00?

## Q18 - Options
(A) 320
(B) 480
(C) 640
(D) 768

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q81

Applying the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion:

1. Let A be the set of 10-bit strings starting with 1:<br>
   Remaining 9 bits can take any value, so \|A\| = 2^9 = 512.
2. Let B be the set of 10-bit strings ending with 00:<br>
   Remaining 8 bits can take any value, so \|B\| = 2^8 = 256.
3. The intersection A ∩ B contains strings starting with 1 and ending with 00:<br>
   Remaining 10 - 3 = 7 bits can take any value, so \|A ∩ B\| = 2^7 = 128.

Total matching bit strings:<br>
\|A ∪ B\| = \|A\| + \|B\| - \|A ∩ B\| = 512 + 256 - 128 = 640.

## Q19
Consider the following statements:<br>
S₁: For any integer n &gt; 1, a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) for all a ∈ Z_n\*, where φ(n) is Euler's phi function.<br>
S₂: If p is prime, then a^p ≡ 1 (mod p) for all a ∈ Z_p\*.

Which one of the following is/are correct?

## Q19 - Options
(A) Only S₁
(B) Only S₂
(C) Both S₁ and S₂
(D) Neither S₁ nor S₂

## Q19 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q94

Evaluating modular arithmetic theorems:

- **S1** is Euler's Totient Theorem: for any integer n &gt; 1 and any integer a coprime to n (a ∈ Z_n\*), a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). This statement is correct.
- **S2** is incorrect. Fermat's Little Theorem states that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p), or a^p ≡ a (mod p). It does not assert a^p ≡ 1 (mod p).

Therefore, only statement S1 is correct.

## Q20
A survey has been conducted on methods of commuter travel. Each respondent was asked to check Bus, Train or Automobile as a major method of travelling to work. More than one answer was permitted. The results reported were as follows :

Bus 30 people; Train 35 people; Automobile 100 people; Bus and Train 15 people; Bus and Automobile 15 people, Train and Automobile 20 people; and all the three methods 5 people.

How many people completed the survey form ?

## Q20 - Options
(A) 160
(B) 165
(C) 115
(D) 120

## Q20 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q34

Applying the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three finite sets determines the total number of survey respondents.

Let B, T, and A represent the sets of commuters using Bus, Train, and Automobile respectively.<br>
\|B ∪ T ∪ A\| = \|B\| + \|T\| + \|A\| - (\|B ∩ T\| + \|B ∩ A\| + \|T ∩ A\|) + \|B ∩ T ∩ A\|

Given data:<br>
\|B\| = 30<br>
\|T\| = 35<br>
\|A\| = 100<br>
\|B ∩ T\| = 15<br>
\|B ∩ A\| = 15<br>
\|T ∩ A\| = 20<br>
\|B ∩ T ∩ A\| = 5

Calculation:<br>
\|B ∪ T ∪ A\| = 30 + 35 + 100 - (15 + 15 + 20) + 5<br>
\|B ∪ T ∪ A\| = 165 - 50 + 5 = 120.

- Hence, exactly 120 people completed the survey form (Option D).

Considering the above definitions, which of the following is not true in the boolean algebra ?

(ii) If x ≤ y and y ≤ x, then x = y<br>
(iii) If x &lt; y and y &lt; z, then x ≤ y<br>
(iv) If x &lt; y and y &lt; z, then x &lt; y

Choose the correct answer from the code given below :<br>
Code :

## Q21 - Options
(A) (iv) only
(B) (ii) and (iii) only
(C) (iii) only
(D) (i) and (ii) only

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Discrete Maths: Counting, Induction, Lattices & Number Theory
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q84

Statement (iii) represents the invalid deduction in the multiple-choice examination context.

- Statements (i) and (ii) state the fundamental properties of partial orders: transitivity and antisymmetry.
